contents:
The competition iLoboke 3v3 robot football: three small robots play against each other inside a fenced field. They have to locate the ball, teammates and opponents using their own vision and communication, then pass, dribble and shoot — no remote control, no human time-outs.
In 2022 we entered two competition circuits: the China Robot and AI Competition (CRAIC) and the RoboCom Developers Competition. We won first prize in the Shanghai region and second prize in the national final at CRAIC, and first prize at the provincial final and third prize at the national final at RoboCom.
My role Implemented low-level motion and decision interfaces in C++, with tactical scripts written in Lua; Worked on passing, shooting and autonomous movement: when to release the ball, where to run, and how to keep three robots from crowding the same spot; Tuned the tactics in simulation first, then on the real field. A perfect pass in simulation becomes something else entirely once friction, latency and localisation error are involved. Takeaways Simulation and reality are separated by uncertainty. In simulation the robot knows the exact position of the ball; on the real field it only has a noisy estimate. A strategy cannot assume it knows — it has to assume it might be wrong and leave room to correct.
Tactics are a team sport, and so is the code. Three robots share one field, so any robot’s decision changes what is optimal for the other two. In the end we stopped writing “what each robot should do” and wrote “what to do given what you see”, letting behaviour emerge from local interactions.
Debugging time is never enough. The window for code changes before a match is short, so parameters had to be adjustable from the sideline and logs had to be replayable. Making failures visible was worth more than writing a smarter strategy.
summary: Three small robots playing autonomously, with passing, shooting and movement strategies written in C++ and Lua.
title: Football robots

contents:
Background MachiKoro is a light, dice-driven strategy board game. The rules are not complicated, but there are many card types and their effects trigger at different moments — a good exercise in object-oriented modelling.
This was a team course project for Algorithms and Programming at Shanghai University in autumn 2022. We built a single-machine Windows console version in C++14, supporting 1-N human players and AI in mixed games.
What we built 15 buildings + 4 landmarks, with complete settlement rules across five card colours Card hierarchy: an abstract Card base class and five subclasses, with action() as a pure virtual function Turn flow: roll dice -> red -> blue/green -> purple -> build one building Two market modes: origin uses all 15 buildings; dlc randomly draws 10 AI play: the AI can roll, choose the number of dice, re-roll and buy on its own Defensive input: regex parsing, single-line input, bounds/funds/duplicate checks My contribution As a team member I worked on core development and debugging, mainly:
the card hierarchy and polymorphic settlement the purchase flow and boundary checks the AI action candidate set input parsing and documentation Outcome The project compiles and runs as a complete game, with mixed human/AI play. Besides the source code, the repository keeps the UML class diagram, course notes, demo videos and the legacy prototype, documenting how it evolved from coursework into a maintainable project.
Source and full documentation: https://github.com/yicongl1/Machikoro
summary: A dice-driven board game in C++14 for 1-N players and AI: 15 buildings, 4 landmarks, five-colour card settlement, market purchases and win conditions.
title: MachiKoro board game in C++

contents:
The competition The “Smart Delivery Drone” event asks a drone to complete a full mission autonomously: fly through obstacles, identify and grasp a target, then release the payload at a designated spot. It is not only about getting airborne — it is about completing a chain of actions reliably without hitting anything or losing the target.
In 2022 our four-person team won first prize at the university qualifier, then represented the university at the 12th Shanghai University Students’ Engineering Practice and Innovation Competition and received the Grand Prize in this event.
My role Responsible for flight-attitude simulation and tuning: validating control parameters in simulation, then transferring them to the real aircraft; Worked with the vision and control teammates to split “obstacle crossing — recognition — grasping — release” into stages that could be debugged independently; The team used Linux, OpenCV, 3D modelling and 3D printing for the control stack and the structural parts of the payload mechanism. Takeaways Make it stable before making it smart. If the attitude is unstable, every downstream vision and grasping problem is amplified into vibration. Time spent tuning is not wasted — it decides whether the mission code ever gets a chance to finish.
Divided work is not separate work. Flight control, vision and structure are tightly coupled: a failed grasp may not be a vision problem at all, but a drifting attitude. A short daily alignment on interfaces and failure symptoms was more effective than everyone debugging in isolation.
Leave a way out for failure. At a competition you usually get one run. Being able to degrade, retry or take over manually is more practical than insisting on full autonomy.
summary: From obstacle crossing and target grasping to payload release — responsible for flight-attitude simulation and tuning, moving control parameters from simulation to the real aircraft.
title: Smart delivery drone
